transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, I guess it’s mostly this memorial I’ve been putting together for my brother. It started out as something simple, you know, just a nice way to honor him, but it’s kind of grown bigger than I meant it to. I’ve been spending most days chasing down songs, calling people, planning displays and even little trips connected to it. My wife says I’ve let the garden and my walking group and, well, just about everything else slide. I don’t mean it in a bad way—I just want it done right.
Have you noticed your mood being unusually high or irritable lately, or maybe that you’re sleeping less than usual but still feel full of energy?

I wouldn’t say “high” exactly… maybe more like, um, fired up? Like I’ll feel really lit up and full of purpose, like this memorial is finally going to make the whole town understand what our family’s been through. That part feels good, honestly.

But then if my wife, or someone at the senior center, slows me down or questions part of the display, I can get sharper than I mean to. I snap sometimes. I know that’s not ideal. I’m not trying to be difficult, Doctor—I just get so focused on doing it right.
Can you tell me if there have been times when you felt more energetic or driven than usual, almost like you couldn’t slow down, even if you wanted to?

Yes… I suppose there have been times like that. I don’t mean I’m trying to overdo it, Doctor, but lately I can’t seem to sit in my chair the way I used to. I’ll get up to move one box, and then I’m hauling three more, making phone calls, sorting papers, then rearranging them all over again.

I sort of pace from room to room, like there’s always one more thing that needs doing. It feels like I’ve got more steam in me than a man my age probably ought to have. That sounds like what you’re asking, doesn’t it?

Doctor: Have you had any distinct period—maybe a few days or more—where your mood was clearly more elevated, irritable, or expansive than usual, almost like a different version of yourself, not just being fired up about the memorial?

Yes… I think so, though I don’t want to make it sound worse than it is. There have been stretches where I feel sort of lit up, like I’m full of purpose and this whole memorial is going to finally make people understand what my family’s been through.

And then, if someone slows me down or questions part of the display—my wife, or someone at the senior center—I can get irritable. I snap before I mean to. It’s not how I want to be, Doctor, but yes, I suppose it does feel like a different version of me at times.
Have there been times when your mood was so unusually upbeat, energetic, or irritable that people around you noticed a clear change in your behavior, separate from your involvement with the memorial?

Yes… I think people have noticed. I don’t mean I’m out of control or anything like that, but my wife has looked at me like I’m… different, I guess.

I’ll feel lit up and full of purpose one minute, like the whole town is finally going to understand our family, and then if she—or someone at the senior center—slows me down or questions the display, I snap. I don’t like admitting that. I’m not trying to be rude. It just comes out sharper than I mean.
Can you think of a time when this elevated or irritable mood lasted for several days in a row, where it wasn’t just about the memorial but affected other parts of your life too?

I suppose… yes, Doctor. It’s not just been one afternoon here or there. It’s been going on, in some form, for about two months now—since my brother passed and I started working on his tribute.

I’ve tried to tell myself it’s just because that matters to me, and I don’t want to make too much of it. But it has carried over into the rest of my days too, not just when I’m directly working on the memorial. Does that make sense?

latest_inference.note: The patient has confirmed a persistent elevated and irritable mood lasting for two months, with clear changes in behavior noticed by others, and not limited to the memorial project. This supports a diagnosis of Bipolar I disorder, current episode manic without psychotic features. The duration and pervasiveness of symptoms rule out a brief hypomanic episode (F30.1), making F31.1 the most appropriate candidate.
